entries.title: Philip Pullman and Maggie O’Farrell among authors urging Burnham to cut business rates on bookshops
entries.summary: After pubs and clubs get rates relief, authors back open letter calling for similar support for bookshops, described as the ‘beating hearts’ of high streetsMaggie O’Farrell, Philip Pullman, Katherine Rundell and Elif Shafak are among the authors supporting a campaign by independent booksellers who have urged Andy Burnham to extend business rates relief for pubs, clubs and live music venues to book
entries.content:
Maggie O’Farrell, Philip Pullman, Katherine Rundell and Elif Shafak are among the authors supporting a campaign by independent booksellers who have urged Andy Burnham to extend business rates relief for pubs, clubs and live music venues to bookshops, warning that rising bills could put some shops at risk of closure.

A total of 234 independent booksellers have signed an open letter organised by the Booksellers Association, calling on the prime minister and the chancellor to give bookshops the same consideration as other businesses that play a significant, positive role in their communities.

The campaign follows the government’s announcement last month of a 20% reduction in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April 2027.

More than a dozen authors have told the Booksellers Association they support the letter, including children’s laureate Patrice Lawrence, Adam Kay, Lemn Sissay, Anthony Horowitz, Patrick Ness, Donna Ashworth and Rachel Joyce.

Burnham also recently announced plans to tackle the spread of vape shops, betting shops and “rogue operators” on high streets, giving local authorities the power to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres. He said such businesses had displaced “the shops, services and community spaces that people are crying out for”.

The letter, sent on 13 August, states that bookshops were “deeply disappointed” to learn they would not be included in the additional relief. “The government has accepted that businesses which deliver significant community benefit deserve targeted support. Bookshops clearly meet that test.”

“Business rates relief for bookshops would also provide a meaningful legacy for the National Year of Reading,” it continued. “The government is rightly telling the country that reading matters. But as things stand, its legacy risks being contradictory: promoting reading on the one hand while implementing policies that reduce investment in bookshops and may contribute to their closure on the other.”

“Independent bookshops are the beating hearts of our high streets and communities”, said O’Farrell, author of Hamnet. “They need all the support we can give them.”

Rundell said: “To lose [bookshops] from our high streets would be to chip away at our culture, and at our ability to access fresh thought and new ideas.”

The Treasury has argued that bookshops already receive support through permanently lower business rates multipliers and a £4.3bn package intended to limit increases in bills.

Analysis commissioned from economic consultancy Cebr found that independent bookshops in England that are not eligible for full small business rates relief face an average annual increase of £4,563 by 2029-30, with some bills expected to double when transitional relief ends.

Across the sector, business rates receipts are projected to increase by 45% nominally. For the average independent bookshop, Cebr estimates this would require selling an extra 1,141 books a year to cover the additional cost.

The impact is already being felt, according to separate Booksellers Association research, with 85% of independent booksellers saying they are less likely to invest in stock, staffing, events or their premises as a result of business rates changes.

“In the current encircling corporate darkness, independent booksellers are lighthouses,” Philip Pullman said. “They are almost the last beacons shining to remind us about private reading, personal discovery, and the life-saving joy of encountering minds and hearts that speak to us as one person to another.”

Laura McCormack, the Booksellers Association’s head of policy and public affairs, said restricting high-street businesses deemed as negative was “only half the job”. “You can’t rebuild Britain’s high streets by tackling the wrong businesses while making it harder for the right ones to succeed,” she said.

entries.title: Christopher Berry-Dee dropped by publisher after allegations of abuse made against him
entries.summary: Bonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigationThe main publisher of the bestselling true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee has dropped the author after a Guardian investigation into allegations of violence and sexual abuse against him, which he denies. Waterstones has also removed his books from sale.“We are shocked and appalled by the ver
entries.content:
The main publisher of the bestselling true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee has dropped the author after a Guardian investigation into allegations of violence and sexual abuse against him, which he denies. Waterstones has also removed his books from sale.

“We are shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations relating to Christopher Berry-Dee, and our thoughts are with those affected,” said the publisher Bonnier Books in a statement to the Guardian.

“Bonnier Books UK will no longer publish Christopher Berry-Dee, we will not work with him on any future projects, and we are terminating all existing agreements”, it continued. “There are practical steps entailed in unwinding longstanding contracts, including those involving third parties, but we are working through them as quickly as we can. We will also be removing our existing stocks from the market.”

An investigation published on Saturday detailed multiple allegations of abuse by Berry-Dee, including domestic violence and sexual assault of a 13-year-old student attending his art school. Berry-Dee refused to be interviewed for the piece, citing health issues, but denied the allegations: “I have not once committed any of the crimes you accuse me of.”

Berry-Dee, 78, is the UK’s top-selling author of true crime. His books, including Talking With Serial Killers, draw on interviews with murderers and have sold nearly 1m copies.

Berry-Dee has admitted lying to his subjects in order to gain access, telling them he intends “to write a book about the miscarriage of justice they are suffering”, he wrote in his 2023 book Talking With Psychopaths and Savages.

Waterstones told the Guardian that Bonnier contacted the bookseller to say that it would no longer publish Berry-Dee’s books. “Following this advice, we have removed the titles from sale in our shops and online,” said a representative.

Orion, an imprint of Hachette, published Inside the Darkest Minds by Berry-Dee last month, but did not respond when asked whether they will continue to publish it.

entries.title: ‘The truth about Diana’: Charles Spencer to publish book about late sister
entries.summary: Earl says he wanted to ‘write down my own thoughts and memories’ with 30th anniversary of Diana’s death ‘on the skyline’Charles Spencer is to publish a book about his sister Diana in September.In the book – titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – Spencer recounts the story of Diana’s life and the week of her death. It marks “the first time that Earl Spencer has spoken openly and at length about his s
entries.content:
Charles Spencer is to publish a book about his sister Diana in September.

In the book – titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – Spencer recounts the story of Diana’s life and the week of her death. It marks “the first time that Earl Spencer has spoken openly and at length about his sister”, according to the book’s publisher, the Penguin imprint Michael Joseph. The book will be released on 22 September in the UK.

“With the 30th anniversary of Diana’s tragic death on the skyline, I’ve been inundated yet again with requests for interviews about my sister,” said Spencer. “This has convinced me to write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time.”

“The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral. As with my eulogy, I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.”

Spencer delivered his sister’s eulogy at Westminster Abbey in September 1997, after her death on 31 August.

Daniel Bunyard, publishing director at Penguin Michael Joseph, said the book contained “many revelations that will draw considerable attention”, but was also “a fitting tribute to the beloved woman who was Princess Diana”.

Spencer said: “I hope this book will be of interest to the many who still cherish the memory of Diana when she was alive.

“I would be delighted if those too young to remember her in her heyday feel, after reading this, that they ‘get’ who she really was: a one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.”

entries.title: Ukrainian Lessons by Charlotte Higgins review – when art and war collide
entries.summary: A vivid and hopeful study of how culture endures in the midst of extreme violenceTowards the end of her subtly piercing book about art in wartime, Charlotte Higgins recounts an autumn visit to Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second city, in the north-east of the country, a short drive from the Russian border. entries.content:
Towards the end of her subtly piercing book about art in wartime, Charlotte Higgins recounts an autumn visit to Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second city, in the north-east of the country, a short drive from the Russian border. In a tranquil park, she sees a man standing in a stream, making stones balance on top of each other in a teetering tower – “a metaphor of life in that city,” she writes, “that would have seemed too obvious for a novel”.

Still, as a good novelist would, Higgins doesn’t seem to beg telling details from a place so much as have them leap to her open eye and ear. The cartoons a boy is watching that fall silent in a power cut, allowing the distant boom of explosions on the frontline to be heard. A cityscape tattooed on a young poet’s arm that cuts off suddenly where skin from his leg was grafted after he was torn up by shrapnel. Cataracts of larkspur, as Higgins describes them, in a field in the frontline Donbas region, “pouring down the hill, pooling at the bottom into a great lake of blooms … Larkspur thrives on ground where there has been recent disturbance.”

This last leads Higgins on to a story her driver tells her about stopping to pee in a roadside ditch and looking down to see the face of a dead Russian soldier staring up at him. The image of the soldier becoming one with the land he was sent to conquer makes her think in turn of a viral video from the early days of the Russian invasion of 2022, in which an old Ukrainian woman thrusts a packet of sunflower seeds on a Russian soldier, urging him to put them in his pockets so that when he is killed, sunflowers will sprout from his body to adorn the Ukrainian soil.

One of the artist heroes of Higgins’s book, Anna Zvyagintseva, designs a bodysuit impregnated with seeds as a piece called Sustainable Costume for an Invader. Another, Marharyta Polovinko, killed in action in 2025 while serving as a drone operator, made macabre pencil drawings about the war, latterly using her own blood as a medium. One of her pictures shows dogs eating a dead Russian soldier. The image, Higgins says is “gruesome, horrific”; she recalls Achilles’s taunt to Hector in The Iliad before he kills him that he will let his body become dog food. “In Polovinko’s hands you sense the image is less about such crude triumphalism and more about the idea of flesh transformed into something else.”

These Ovidian metamorphoses lean into the ancient Greek strand of the book, where Higgins, a classicist as well as the Guardian’s chief culture writer, aligns Greek myth and the characters drawn by Homer and Aeschylus with the present-day choices and agonies of mortal Ukrainians. But such explicit transformations are subsidiary to her main matter, the metamorphoses of artists and art itself under conditions of war.

In a city near the frontline she meets Yaroslav Pilunskiy, a cinematographer from the Kyiv-based film collective Babylon 13, now working drones for the army. Little remains for him of his art. Once in a while, when there’s a nice sunset, he flies a drone to a lake where explosions are guaranteed, just for the visuals, but otherwise he’s been transformed into a 21st-century drone soldier. On the eve of the invasion, he was in Rome, editing a film; by the time Higgins meets him, 19 months later, he can’t remember what it was. “Sometimes,” Higgins writes, “he felt he had imagined it all.”

Higgins quotes Diana Berg, a cultural manager and activist twice forced to flee from eastern Ukrainian cities: “Until the war is over, the best conceptual artists in Ukraine are the army.” And the still bleaker words of the poet Halyna Kruk: “There is no place for poetry when you spend several days standing next to the collapsed basement of a high-rise building, hearing your children and grandchildren screaming under the rubble, and you cannot rescue them.” She regretted, she concluded, that poets could not take their verse to battle as literal weapons. “I’m sorry that poetry doesn’t kill.”

Higgins undergoes her own metamorphosis, from arts correspondent to something like a war correspondent interviewing artists, as her curiosity takes her much closer to the actual fighting than she expected in the beginning. Russia’s promiscuous use of missiles and drones against Ukrainian cities, anyway, means that the whole of Ukraine is a frontline and, like most visitors to Kyiv, Higgins gets caught up in air raids. For much of the book the war is noises off stage, but the violence is so deep and wide that every so often a small parenthesis drops with force: the building where 50 people were killed, the conductor shot dead because he refused to take part in an occupation concert. Most devastatingly, one of the writers Higgins grows closest to is killed in a Russian missile attack.

Higgins, present but not obtrusive in her account, says that her time in Ukraine “unanchored” her. “It altered and enlarged the way I saw things, as if I had been given different eyes.”

Part of the change she imposes on herself is learning Ukrainian, at a time when Ukrainians are struggling with the fact that for many loyal anti-Putin Ukrainians, Russian is still their first language. The backlash against Russian culture in free Ukraine is fierce. Statues of Pushkin, once common enough, are now deemed signs of a hostile power marking its territory. Higgins quotes an essay by the writer and editor Sasha Dovzhyk: “Russian is my mother tongue and liberation means ripping it out of my throat.”

Despite Berg and Kruk’s rageous words, Higgins finds that the artists, poets, diarists, novelists and film-makers she meets still find ways and reasons to create. Indeed, she writes, “the argument of this book is that the literature and art made by these people, some of whom have lost their lives, will shape the war’s memory”. It’s a strong claim, in a world where the meme makers and clip aggregators often seem to have usurped even the historian and the balladeer, let alone the writer and artist. But the impression left by Higgins’s vivid and hopeful book is one of a multitude of creative ripples spreading and overlapping through Ukrainians’ wartime consciousness. There is solace in art; here are ways to describe the incomprehensible; here is, if not your memory, at least my record.

“For me, there is no sense in writing about war,” Artur Dron’, the poet and wounded soldier with the interrupted tattoo, tells Higgins. “But it’s very important to write about people. That’s my focus: not trenches or shelling, not rockets, bullets or guns. I went through it; I don’t want to write about it. The main thing is to write about how we can save our sense of love in the trenches.”

Never, writes Higgins, has she seen people listening with such intensity to poetry as she did in a (literally) underground bar in Kharkiv in 2025. “The people in the audience were straining forward, caught up in the deeply felt present, of communal listening, and the sense of inchoate emotions being articulated. When the famous Kharkiv novelist, poet and now soldier Serhiy Zhadan read his work, I saw a woman in the audience mouthing the words along with him, because she knew his poems by heart.”

entries.title: Sunrise by Téa Obreht review – secrets and myths in the American west
entries.summary: Set across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recordedTéa Obreht’s novels teem with conflicting narratives, treacherous landscapes and speculative fictions. Her 2010 prizewinning debut, The Tiger’s Wife, examined themes of death, miracles and outsider status in the midst of a fictional Balkan war. Her fourth no
entries.content:
Téa Obreht’s novels teem with conflicting narratives, treacherous landscapes and speculative fictions. Her 2010 prizewinning debut, The Tiger’s Wife, examined themes of death, miracles and outsider status in the midst of a fictional Balkan war. Her fourth novel, Sunrise, returns to a western frontier haunted by ghosts and stalked by outlaws, a territory Obreht first explored in her second book, Inland.

It is August 2024. Nina Terzic has just jumped – or was she pushed? – from a crash-landing Cessna into a lake somewhere in the mountains of Wyoming. She manages to swim to shore. There is no sign of her boyfriend Ben, who was in the plane with her, and her phone – though miraculously intact – has no signal. Nina, a postgraduate student, was supposed to be on holiday from her job as a live-in nanny in New York. We get the feeling that her relationship with Ben might have a darker underside.

Nina quickly realises that she has happened upon a ghost town, one of the dozens of abandoned mining settlements scattered across the Old West. Exploring her surroundings further, she discovers the body of a woman hidden in a cellar. Beside the dead woman is a backpack containing a manuscript.

The sequence that follows is a part of that manuscript. Its action takes place in 1902, in the mountain town of Sunrise – the ghost town as it was, before everyone left. A man named Anton Vargas has returned after a long absence. He carries with him an aura of celebrity – or is it notoriety? Only Fred Kipley, the town’s deputy, seems unsurprised to see him again. Kipley and Vargas were once involved in a shootout with local bandits. Their courageous actions saved lives and cast them as heroes; in the years since, their exploits have become the stuff of dime-store novels and wild west shows. But Vargas is not a well man, and he has business to settle in town before it is too late.

The novel’s central section moves us a century forward to 2003. Sunrise is now a ghost town, the haunt of tourists. We meet Colin Yard, whose re-enactments of the Vargas story have become a valued source of income. Coll is greatly invested not only in Vargas’s story but in himself as the rightful guardian of that story. When he is contacted by a writer, Louise Hawley, asking if he will read the novel she has written about Vargas, Coll doesn’t pay her much attention. But Louise has her own deep-rooted connection with the place, and has discovered new information about Sunrise’s local hero that casts his story in a radically different light.

Coll is furious at what he sees as her trespass: “We have this small thing, you know?… This tiny part of history that belongs to us. And I don’t want it to be fucked with or misinterpreted by someone who, frankly, doesn’t understand it or care about it.” Louise is adamant that the material she has unearthed deserves to be scrutinised. She argues that Coll himself has altered material facts to fit his re-enactments, that recorded history is by its nature partly fictitious. But for Coll, “his” Vargas is the only Vargas. How far will he be willing to go to protect his property?

It is in this section that the novel’s themes and intertwined relationships come most persuasively to life. To Louise, Coll’s home town seems idyllic, the kind of place where neighbours are as good as family. But the situation is more fraught than surface impressions might suggest. Coll has recently had a disturbing altercation with the local bad boy, Bob Fournier. “Bob’s latest madness” is considered an outrage, yet no one has it in them to go up against him. Coll’s tacit condoning of Fournier’s actions has terrible consequences – not least for himself – but it is symptomatic also of a moral cowardice that will indirectly precipitate a greater calamity.

Obreht’s portrayal of Colin Yard – his gradual, desperate slide from favoured son to villain of the piece – is a brilliant piece of theatre. Coll’s attempt to control the narrative is echoed in the bullying paternalism of John Daisy, the villain of Louise’s novel, a rich landowner and stockman whose “big house” casts its shadow over Sunrise back in 1902. Daisy is an avid collector of Native American artefacts and a supposed authority on Native traditions – too bad if his patronage does not extend to living people. Throughout all three of her interwoven timelines, Obreht raises similarly searching questions about courage and cowardice, idealism and pragmatism, and most of all about how history is recounted and who gets to own it.

The novel does have its flaws. While the eventual revelations about Nina’s relationship with the ghastly Ben feel devastatingly real, it is difficult to ignore the loopholes in logic that characterise Nina’s portions of the narrative: how is she able to fall from a height on to water without getting injured? Having survived the crash unscathed, why does she waste time – and phone charge – trying to text her mother when she should be looking for a signal and calling 911? None of this detracts from the fact that Sunrise is an engrossing, original and thought-provoking novel, effortlessly readable and beautifully told. Given that most of what we come to know about Vargas is itself a series of fictions, it perhaps makes better sense to frame Nina’s miraculous survival as similarly mythic.

entries.title: Agrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient Rome
entries.summary: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for powerIf you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week, Robert Harris has you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assas
entries.content:
If you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week, Robert Harris has you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assassination of Julius Caesar, with all the bickering and bloodshed that follows, on to the decisive battle of Actium and Octavius’s apotheosis as Caesar Augustus. We meet Cicero, Fulvia, Lepidus, two Caesars and a burly Antony (“Imagine, if you will, a statue of Hercules with a club in one hand, a wineskin in the other”).

Here’s the clever bit: he narrates it all from the point of view of Octavius’s right-hand man, Agrippa, a much less well-remembered figure. Harris tells us he “left behind no speeches, few letters and only a couple of sentences of direct quotation”. Yet Agrippa was “effective co-ruler of the Roman world for many years” and “the greatest general of the period”. Octavius couldn’t have risen without him, but he seems to have done his best to write him out of the story afterwards, according him only two passing mentions in the Res Gestae Divi Augusti.

Harris’s Octavius is vain, clever, sickly, ambitious, manipulative and prickly. His childhood friend Agrippa, the only person he sort-of trusts, is established early on as a bit of a meathead. Their first encounter is when Agrippa duffs up a couple of bullies he catches picking on a weaker boy; mostly for the pleasure of duffing a couple of people up. He doesn’t know at the time that the beneficiary of this duffing is Caesar’s nephew. They become friends: “He helped me with my classwork. I showed him how to fight.” They share a teacher: “He instilled in Octavius especially a lifelong love of poetry, although my literary tastes, to his despair, have always tended towards works on engineering and military history.” Even as they rise to power, our man’s eye is on the duffing. Octavius returns to Rome amid great danger to give a rousing speech, and Agrippa reports only: “His voice carried well. I did not pay much attention to what he said. I was too preoccupied scanning his audience for potential assassins.”

Harris’s framing conceit is that the text we are reading is Agrippa’s memoir, written in some haste and high feeling. Agrippa, now an old man of 50, has come home early from an expedition to duff up the barbarians in Illyricum. He has a gammy leg, which is about to kill him. He limps in to find his wife in bed with his son-in-law. Since the son-in-law is also the emperor’s adopted son, he hesitates to get busy with his sword and instead retreats to his chamber. He’s feeling a bit sorry for himself and, uncharacteristically, he turns to words.

It is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious prose. There’s a lot of pipe-laying in the military history department, of the “then the legions would wheel around the far side of the Black Sea by way of Hyrcania, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, and march west” type. And he’s a bastard for an aqueduct, is Agrippa. Loves them; maybe even more than having a scrap. He’s never happier than when building infrastructure and explaining the engineering principles and logistics to the reader.

When Agrippa is stirred to reflection, he tends to reach for a well-worn phrase. “The sickly, pungent stink of death lurked round every corner.” “Mercy was now the order of the day.” “War, which I had once so relished, was gouged into the countryside like an open wound.” “Power makes monsters of us all.” “In the words of the old saying – if you strike at the king, you must be sure not to miss.” (That particular old saying, I think, comes from The Wire, but never mind.)

But from all this elegantly drab stuff emerges a more subtle portrait of the man and the age than you might expect. You get a persuasive portrait of a Rome exhausted by civil strife, and of the serpentine manoeuvrings of its rulers. Everyone is betraying everyone else, raising armies, marrying each other’s children, forming and breaking alliances. It’s hectic. And, gosh, all these people redrawing the map of the world and changing the course of history are young. The plot twist – a feature of scholarly speculation since 1937, Harris’s afterword tells us – concerns the real parentage of the apparently low-born Agrippa.

But that, like much else, it suited him to keep quiet about. His most enduring real-world monument is seven terse words in stone above the entrance to the Pantheon: M F AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIUM FECIT. “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, in his third consulship, did it.”

entries.title: The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatments
entries.summary: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted himWhich, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you d
entries.content:
Which, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you don’t have to choose between them. He’s all five wrapped into one objectionable package, and so much more besides.

The tale begins with the Sonoran desert toad, an improbable amphibian that spends most of its life hiding underground in the baking badlands along the Mexico-Arizona border, and has done so blamelessly for millions of years. Whenever it rains, the toads emerge from their hiding places to mate, laying strings of eggs wherever water has pooled.

There have long been fanciful tales of hippies getting high by licking toads, but these ones are the real deal: the world’s only known psychoactive animal. In the early 1980s, humans discovered that the toad’s poison glands secrete a venom that contains, among other chemicals, 5-MeO-DMT, a potent hallucinogen also known as the “God molecule”. The first known user squirted the glands of a toad that his dog caught on to the windscreen of his Chevy Sport, where the substance dried and he smoked it.

He wrote a manual describing “an overload of thoughts and perception, brief collapse of the ego, and loss of the space-time continuum”. It was, in short, a lot. The prospect enticed other users, and those included, two decades later, Rettig.

A troubled young man from Mexico, Rettig started smoking dried toad venom in the first decade of this century, and claims it helped him kick his crack cocaine habit. That was a time when popular interest in psychedelics was re-emerging after the long post-1960s winter, and many medical practitioners were wondering if these mind-altering chemicals couldn’t help patients who weren’t responding to their traditional treatments. Much of the focus had been on LSD, psilocybin and ketamine, but 5-MeO-DMT provided a whole new level of experience. The shatteringly powerful effect of the chemical was said to replicate the effect of years of therapy in just half an hour, which is clearly an attractive prospect for a psychedelic entrepreneur keen to maximise patient throughput.

Rettig was no pioneer in his enthusiasm for smoking toad. Instead, his contribution was to create a tradition for this new hallucinogen, thus giving it the kind of mystical authenticity that peyote, morning glory and ayahuasca gain among devotees thanks to their association with ancient Native American rituals.

The Seri people, who live between the Sonoran Desert and the Gulf of California, have suffered terribly both under the Spanish colony of Mexico, and the independent republic. By the time Rettig visited in 2011, there were just a few hundred of them left, living in squalid and trash-strewn villages, predated upon by drug cartels and plagued by addiction. Rettig adopted their chants, claimed their ancient toad-based tradition had been suppressed and was only now being rediscovered, and started presenting himself globally as a practitioner of indigenous medicine.

There may well be a medical case for treatment with 5-MeO-DMT, but it’s hard to see any argument for treating people with it the way that Rettig did. He offered huge doses with minimal screening, sometimes inflicting treatment forcibly. (In response to footage of him being aggressive to clients, he told De Greef: “I am open to acknowledge that some of my actions might be disturbing for most audiences, but this is a very deep therapeutic work.”) He engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakes. Rettig claims: “My work has been misunderstood, misinterpreted, and misused.” But it is an incredibly dark tale.

A different writer might have been tempted to go gonzo, to smoke toad himself, and to come back with stories of ego death, the space-time continuum and the rest of it, but Kimon de Greef mercifully avoids that temptation. A South African, he came to the story of Rettig not from the world of psychedelics but from researching wildlife smuggling, which gives him an unusually clear-eyed view of how grim these kinds of practices are.

A lot of the reporting for this book began life in the New Yorker, and it is as methodical, exacting, well-written and exceptionally reported as you’d expect. Fortunately, De Greef avoids the fate that can befall books based on American magazine articles that fail to break free of them, and really enjoys the extra space. He launches into entertaining digressions into how exactly the toads’ psychedelic powers were first discovered, into how pharmaceutical companies are harnessing 5-MeO-DMT for their own ends, introducing fascinating cameos, before he returns to the main story.

He is not a man for grand conclusions, but I challenge any reader not to see this highly enjoyable book as a parable for so much that’s wrong with the current economy. Everything from the undeserved authority of charlatans, to the rampant exploitation of the natural world, to the hiding of hyper-capitalism behind a shield of cod-mystical woo-woo: it’s all in there.

Rettig’s ultimate fate has been to be largely forgotten by the movement he helped to popularise, which has mutated and expanded at the speed of social media, with new influencers appearing and new markets opening. The toads, meanwhile, have become just another commodity to be exploited.
